title: Exact integer and floating bit serialization, with explicit failure conditions
explanation: byteorder-lite 0.1.0: fixed-width unsigned and signed integer writes, plus BE/LE write_f32/write_f64, write their exact bit representations in the selected endian order and preserve trailing bytes when the output is long enough; shorter buffers panic before writing. Float proofs quantify over every 32/64-bit representation, including NaN payloads and signed zeros, under explicit bit-pattern and std to_bits models. No floating arithmetic is modeled. Signed write_i24 and write_int additionally serialize the low 24 or 8*nbytes bits for every signed input value, preserving suffix bytes; no signed representability condition is required. Invalid byte counts or short buffers panic as specified. Signed read_int/read_i24 additionally return the exact two-complement prefix decode at the selected width; all invalid counts and short inputs assert before sign extension. LittleEndian from_slice_u16/u32/u64/u128 and from_slice_i16/i32/i64/i128 additionally leave every slice unchanged on the verified little-endian target, including empty slices and all element values. Native LittleEndian from_slice_f32/f64 also preserve every memory bit under the existing representations, including NaN payloads and signed zeros; this is not a Rust floating PartialEq claim. The two handwritten Default methods always panic. The four variable-width unsigned writers additionally have exact byte-count/space guards, selected-byte output on success and assertion failure otherwise. Unsigned 24-bit readers/writers additionally have exact 3-byte decoding/serialization, a 24-bit value domain and complete short-buffer/value-overflow failures. Four unsigned variable-width readers decode the exact selected prefix under their complete byte-count/input-length guard, and assert otherwise. Eight concrete original 48-bit default methods are also verified: unsigned reads decode six bytes below 2^48; unsigned writes require a value below 2^48; signed reads decode six-byte two-complement values; signed writes truncate every i64 input to its low 48 bits. Enough buffer space preserves the suffix; short buffers fail assertion. Each original default body is connected by definitional equality to its original concrete general-width callee with count six. BE/LE read_int128 and write_int128 also cover all values and counts: signed reads decode the selected prefix for counts1..16 with enough input and assert otherwise; signed writes serialize the low8*count bits of every i128, preserving suffix bytes. Invalid write counts0 or above16 fail integerOverflow in unextend_sign128 before the writer; valid counts with insufficient output assert. Actual original unsigned128 callees are linked by definitional equality to existing general contracts; original extend_sign128/unextend_sign128 bodies are proved directly with no new models.
trusted_assumptions: F32/F64 are explicit 32/64-bit logical patterns; two executable std to_bits models preserve those patterns as unsigned words, with checked Lean value-preservation lemmas. Guards require original writer bodies and allow no other float operation. Kani checks std bit identity for every pattern and actual released writers with 6/10-byte buffers. Connecting these Rust checks to the Lean representation is reviewed, not mechanized; Rust nightlies differ. Official translation/standard integer and slice models, Lean, and Kani/CBMC are trusted. The ten native conversion bodies make no external calls after official target-branch translation. Thirteen native-path declarations remain in the unchanged, unimported external template. The native provider imports the existing bit-pattern representation module and supplies zero new definitions or operation models; native bodies invoke no external operation. Existing to_bits models remain used by the earlier float writers only. Guards require exactly the original identity bodies and zero external use. Mapped audits permit only propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound.
environment: Archive-identical Rust/Cargo.toml; x86_64 default features, debug extraction. Rust nightly-2026-09-17, Charon08d7c9d50144bd84848212c24701253585e90d1f, Aeneas be86ab0f1989d04944292b345b24c435be3ad10a, Lean4.35.0. Kani0.68.0/CBMC6.11.0/Rust nightly-2026-08-21: six harnesses, 276 checks, no failures per crate.
limitations: This covers 36 selected writer methods, sixteen scoped integer readers, ten native-target identity conversions, and two handwritten Default methods, not all public APIs. Fixed-width 16/32/64/128-bit reads, other bulk and in-place conversions, I/O extensions, other targets and release extraction remain unproved. The float result establishes bit serialization only: floating arithmetic, comparisons, rounding, numeric accuracy, NaN arithmetic and signaling behavior are not modeled. Kani public-writer buffer lengths are fixed at 6 and 10; arbitrary valid slice lengths are quantified separately by the Lean theorems. The write_int documentation says nonrepresentable values panic, while original-body theorems establish truncation for all i64 inputs when count/space guards hold; 176 finite native observations corroborate selected boundaries. This is a documentation/behavior mismatch, not a memory-safety finding. write_i24 documents only short-buffer panic and is not classified as a documentation problem. Other signed reads remain unproved. Opposite-endian conversion methods and other target configurations are not covered by the identity results. Panic messages and unwinding side effects are not specified. Separately, write_int128 documentation also says a nonrepresentable value panics; the original-body Lean theorem establishes truncation for all i128 inputs under valid count/space guards. This additional documentation contrast follows from the proof and source text, with no new native observation claimed; the176 native observations remain specific to the prior signed64/24 investigation.
tool_limitations: Lean backend only, requiring cargo-proofs 0.4.0 or later. The version identifies the official Aeneas Git revision pinned in lake-manifest.json (backends/lean); this revision uses Lean 4.35.0. The recorder checks committed Lean theorem declarations and permits only propext, Classical.choice, and Quot.sound as transitive axioms. It rejects sorryAx and custom axioms, including axiomatized external models. Charon/Aeneas extraction is not rerun. The author must review that the committed functional model matches the recorded Rust source, that the named theorem corresponds to the public API, and that the reported precondition matches the theorem. A checked theorem alone does not establish those links or the adequacy of the specification. The current adapter records the default Cargo configuration, with ordinary Lean module paths and a pinned official Git dependency. Other backends, custom Lake source directories, and local-path Aeneas dependencies are unsupported. See https://proofs.rs/book/aeneas.html and https://github.com/AeneasVerif/aeneas/tree/be86ab0f1989d04944292b345b24c435be3ad10a.

claims.title: Verification of <byteorder_lite::BigEndian as byteorder_lite::ByteOrder>::write_i128 (with Aeneas be86ab0f1989d04944292b345b24c435be3ad10a)
claims.precondition: Arbitrary well-typed integer and byte slice on x86_64 with default features; both sufficient-buffer normal return and short-buffer panic are specified.
claims.report_title: Exact integer and floating bit serialization, with explicit failure conditions
claims.shared_explanation: byteorder-lite 0.1.0: fixed-width unsigned and signed integer writes, plus BE/LE write_f32/write_f64, write their exact bit representations in the selected endian order and preserve trailing bytes when the output is long enough; shorter buffers panic before writing. Float proofs quantify over every 32/64-bit representation, including NaN payloads and signed zeros, under explicit bit-pattern and std to_bits models. No floating arithmetic is modeled. Signed write_i24 and write_int additionally serialize the low 24 or 8*nbytes bits for every signed input value, preserving suffix bytes; no signed representability condition is required. Invalid byte counts or short buffers panic as specified. Signed read_int/read_i24 additionally return the exact two-complement prefix decode at the selected width; all invalid counts and short inputs assert before sign extension. LittleEndian from_slice_u16/u32/u64/u128 and from_slice_i16/i32/i64/i128 additionally leave every slice unchanged on the verified little-endian target, including empty slices and all element values. Native LittleEndian from_slice_f32/f64 also preserve every memory bit under the existing representations, including NaN payloads and signed zeros; this is not a Rust floating PartialEq claim. The two handwritten Default methods always panic. The four variable-width unsigned writers additionally have exact byte-count/space guards, selected-byte output on success and assertion failure otherwise. Unsigned 24-bit readers/writers additionally have exact 3-byte decoding/serialization, a 24-bit value domain and complete short-buffer/value-overflow failures. Four unsigned variable-width readers decode the exact selected prefix under their complete byte-count/input-length guard, and assert otherwise. Eight concrete original 48-bit default methods are also verified: unsigned reads decode six bytes below 2^48; unsigned writes require a value below 2^48; signed reads decode six-byte two-complement values; signed writes truncate every i64 input to its low 48 bits. Enough buffer space preserves the suffix; short buffers fail assertion. Each original default body is connected by definitional equality to its original concrete general-width callee with count six. BE/LE read_int128 and write_int128 also cover all values and counts: signed reads decode the selected prefix for counts1..16 with enough input and assert otherwise; signed writes serialize the low8*count bits of every i128, preserving suffix bytes. Invalid write counts0 or above16 fail integerOverflow in unextend_sign128 before the writer; valid counts with insufficient output assert. Actual original unsigned128 callees are linked by definitional equality to existing general contracts; original extend_sign128/unextend_sign128 bodies are proved directly with no new models.
claims.shared_trusted_assumptions: F32/F64 are explicit 32/64-bit logical patterns; two executable std to_bits models preserve those patterns as unsigned words, with checked Lean value-preservation lemmas. Guards require original writer bodies and allow no other float operation. Kani checks std bit identity for every pattern and actual released writers with 6/10-byte buffers. Connecting these Rust checks to the Lean representation is reviewed, not mechanized; Rust nightlies differ. Official translation/standard integer and slice models, Lean, and Kani/CBMC are trusted. The ten native conversion bodies make no external calls after official target-branch translation. Thirteen native-path declarations remain in the unchanged, unimported external template. The native provider imports the existing bit-pattern representation module and supplies zero new definitions or operation models; native bodies invoke no external operation. Existing to_bits models remain used by the earlier float writers only. Guards require exactly the original identity bodies and zero external use. Mapped audits permit only propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound.
claims.shared_limitations: This covers 36 selected writer methods, sixteen scoped integer readers, ten native-target identity conversions, and two handwritten Default methods, not all public APIs. Fixed-width 16/32/64/128-bit reads, other bulk and in-place conversions, I/O extensions, other targets and release extraction remain unproved. The float result establishes bit serialization only: floating arithmetic, comparisons, rounding, numeric accuracy, NaN arithmetic and signaling behavior are not modeled. Kani public-writer buffer lengths are fixed at 6 and 10; arbitrary valid slice lengths are quantified separately by the Lean theorems. The write_int documentation says nonrepresentable values panic, while original-body theorems establish truncation for all i64 inputs when count/space guards hold; 176 finite native observations corroborate selected boundaries. This is a documentation/behavior mismatch, not a memory-safety finding. write_i24 documents only short-buffer panic and is not classified as a documentation problem. Other signed reads remain unproved. Opposite-endian conversion methods and other target configurations are not covered by the identity results. Panic messages and unwinding side effects are not specified. Separately, write_int128 documentation also says a nonrepresentable value panics; the original-body Lean theorem establishes truncation for all i128 inputs under valid count/space guards. This additional documentation contrast follows from the proof and source text, with no new native observation claimed; the176 native observations remain specific to the prior signed64/24 investigation.
